title: Why Does Student Motivation Matter? And Whose Job Is It, Anyway?
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart opens a series on noncognitive factors by asking two questions: whose job is student motivation, and motivation toward what? He answers the first with a shared-responsibility view in which students, parents and teachers all shape the conditions, warning against teachers who take all or none of the blame. He answers the second by arguing that the shared purpose of schools is the long-term flourishing of students, with passing, graduating and college readiness as steps rather than ultimate goals. He also defends the term noncognitive factors as imperfect but the best available label for a mix of beliefs, attitudes and behaviors. The piece sets the purposeful frame for the research that follows.
points: Motivation depends on many sources, so placing all responsibility on teacher or student is a pathology.
The ultimate aim shared across subjects is long-term flourishing, which makes college and career readiness an indicator rather than the destination.
Compliance-driven motivation (do the work, pass, graduate) is called important but boring and not ultimate.
Noncognitive factors are defined as a cornucopia of beliefs, attitudes and behaviors, some of them intensely cognitive, which is why the label is awkward but still useful.
quotes: The problem with the phrase “Leverage Noncognitive Factors” is that it sounds super boring. Also, it’s pretty misleading; some of the “noncognitive” factors are intensely cognitive.

Such pathologies require an awareness of how intricate motivation is — how it depends not on a single source or factor, but upon many. D), then, is quite right because students, parents, and teachers all play a role in creating conditions that either lends themselves to or inhibit motivation.

If we want them to be motivated just so they’ll do our work and pass our class or get our diploma, then I find studying student motivation to be pretty boring. All of these things are important — I want my students (and my children) to, at the very least, do their work and pass their classes and graduate from high school — but they aren’t ultimate.
I believe that ultimately, schools exist to promote the long-term flourishing of their students; this is our one shared, enduring standard.

Teaching toward long-term flourishing is different from, say, teaching toward college. I do teach toward career- and college-readiness (CCR) on a daily basis — in fact, the NFO Framework was born during my study of the most widespread CCR standards, the Common Core — but these things are steps on the journey to long-term flourishing. Such readiness is not the sole point of secondary schooling, even though they are a precious indicator of whether or not our secondary schooling is doing what it should.
